title: Monte Carlo Methods — Learning from Complete Episodes

questions.question: You cannot query the dynamics of your robot, but you can run it and record what happened. What is the simplest estimator of V^π(s)?
options: Fit a model of the dynamics first, then run value iteration on it
Take the max over actions of the rewards observed at s
Average the observed returns that followed visits to s
Regress reward on state features with supervised learning
questions.explanation: V^π is defined as an expected return, and a sample mean is the plainest estimator of an expectation. The only capability required is the ability to sample episodes.

questions.question: How do first-visit and every-visit Monte Carlo differ statistically?
options: First-visit is biased at finite sample size; every-visit is unbiased throughout
First-visit is unbiased at any episode count; every-visit is biased but consistent
Both are unbiased estimators and differ only in the variance they carry
Every-visit estimates Q* while first-visit estimates V^π for whatever policy generated the data
questions.explanation: One sample per episode keeps first-visit returns iid. Repeat visits inside a single episode are correlated, which is exactly where every-visit's finite-sample bias comes from.

questions.question: The incremental mean is V_n = V_{n-1} + (1/n)[G_n − V_{n-1}]. What happens if you swap 1/n for a constant α?
options: You get an exponentially-weighted estimate that tracks changes in π
The estimate stops converging at all, since 1/n is required by Robbins-Monro
It silently becomes an every-visit estimator
It silently becomes a first-visit estimator
questions.explanation: A constant step size forgets old returns geometrically, which is what you want once π keeps changing. That single substitution is the step from MC to TD to every modern RL update.

questions.question: Why compute returns with the backward recurrence G_t = r_{t+1} + γ G_{t+1} instead of summing each suffix directly?
options: It removes the discount from the estimate
It lets the method handle episodes that never terminate
It produces all T returns in a single O(T) pass
It is what makes the resulting estimator unbiased
questions.explanation: It is a pure computational reorganization of the same discounted sum. Summing each suffix independently costs O(T²) and gives identical numbers.

questions.question: Your MC control agent acts greedily on a freshly zeroed Q and never improves. What is the diagnosis?
options: γ is too high, so credit assignment across the episode is too noisy to learn from
Ties in Q pin it to one action, so the rest go unsampled
First-visit MC is biased at low episode counts
The returns need to be normalized before the update
questions.explanation: MC only ever sees the state-action pairs the policy visits. Without ε-greedy or exploring starts, whole regions keep their initial estimates permanently.

questions.question: Your MC estimate of V^π(0,0) for the uniform policy on the deterministic 4×4 grid sits near -39, but the previous lesson's value iteration printed -6.43. What is the right read?
options: MC has not converged and simply needs a far larger episode budget
MC is biased upward by the importance-sampling weights
They describe a different policy on a different grid
The two runs must be using different discount factors
questions.explanation: -6.43 is V* on the slippery grid. The matching reference for this estimate is iterative policy evaluation of the same uniform policy on the same deterministic grid, about -39.4.
